lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 3 you met line plots with halves and quarters. On a line plot, what does each X stand for? One thing that was measured.
A line plot shows data on a number line. Each X is one thing that was measured: here, each X is one stick.
Read a line plot by counting the Xs: in this one, 3 sticks are 2/4 m long and 1 stick is 3/4 m long.
Find the difference between the longest and the shortest stick by taking away: 3/4 − 1/4 = 2/4 m.
Add lengths to put sticks end to end: two sticks of 1/4 m make a line 2/4 m long.
Try it in the world: measure 6 sticks or planks in quarters of a metre and draw a line plot. Which length has the most Xs? Next: angles.

exercises.prompt: How many sticks are 3/8 m long?
How many sticks are longer than 4/8 m?
exercises.hint: Count the Xs to the right of 4/8.
exercises.explain: 1 stick is 5/8 m and 3 are 6/8 m: 4 sticks.

exercises.hint: Every X is one stick: count them all.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference in length between the longest and the shortest stick, in metres?
exercises.hint: The longest is 6/8 m and the shortest 2/8 m.

exercises.prompt: Which length is the most common?
exercises.hint: Which length has the most Xs?

exercises.prompt: All the 6/8 m sticks are laid end to end. How long is the line, in metres?
Together, the two 2/8 m sticks are as long as one 4/8 m stick.
Sort the lengths: more than 1/2 m, or not?
exercises.hint: 2/4 is the same as 1/2. Compare the quarters with 2/4.
exercises.explain: 3/4 m and 4/4 m are more than 1/2 m. 1/4 m is less, and 2/4 m is exactly 1/2 m.
